newsitem.title: MEXICO: FEATURE - Fortified tortillas give life to Mexicans.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Fortified tortillas give life to Mexicans.

text.p: The children of El Rincon San Ildefonso have an extra spring in their step these days and, more importantly, fewer are dying.

That is the prelimary conclusion from a pilot program to improve nutrition in poor, rural areas where the staple of the family diet is the tortilla -- a round, flat corn pancake first eaten by native Indians perhaps 3,000 years ago.

If the pilot results prove conclusive, and if the $17 million in needed funding is found, the program could spread to 13 areas of Mexico where malnutrition is particularly acute, the program's director said.

"The kids really were different. They're running, playing," said Adolfo Chavez, a physician with the National Nutrition Institute and director of the tortilla-enrichment experiment. "It's a marked difference from the rural child who cries and hits his mother, which are part of the syndrome that I call malnutrition."
Otomi Indian children at a school in El Rincon are living proof, each a bundle of energy showing off for visitors during a recent session of physical education.
Experts from the United States and Europe will gather in Mexico City on Oct. 24 to judge the results of the program.

Malnutrition stunts physical, mental and social development of children, said Chavez, who estimates 2.2 million Mexican children from four million families are malnourished. What is worse, 80 percent of all Mexicans are born into the poorest 20 percent of families, Chavez said. "They are going to be 80 percent of all future Mexicans."

For poor villages like El Rincon, part of the municipality of Amealco about 90 miles (150 km) north of Mexico City, tortillas are often the only thing people eat, occasionally with a bit of nopal cactus.

Grupo Industrial Maseca, Mexico's leading producer of corn-flour and tortillas, is donating eight tonnes of corn flour every two weeks to the pilot program. Half is enriched with soy, vitamins and minerals and destined for communities like El Rincon, a village of some 700 people, mostly Otomi Indians who sometimes line up for nearly an hour to receive their bounty. The other half, unfortified corn flour, goes to other poor communities.

Children from both groups are monitored every two weeks with blood and urine samples and weight and height measurements. One startling result: children eating enriched tortillas are growing three times as fast as the others, Chavez said.
And, according to life-long tortilla-eaters here, nobody can taste the difference.

Before the program began in November, about two children a month were dying of diseases linked directly or indirectly to malnutrition, said Gerardo Rodriguez Hernandez, the institute's caseworker in El Rincon. Since then "we have not had one single death of a child under five years old and that's one way we can measure the impact of our program," he told Reuters after distributing fortified corn flour to the Otomi Indians.

El Rincon, like many rural areas in Mexico, has virtually no job opportunities and poor soil in which to grow crops. For Tomas Chavez, the father of one family benefiting from the super tortillas, the program means survival. "Here we're all poor," he told Reuters. "We don't have anything, much less a chance to work. I mean, we're lucky to find a few centavos. It's good that they're helping us. It's important."

There are side benefits as well. Women are spared the grueling task of waking before dawn to boil and grind corn by hand. With corn flour produced in high-tech plants, all they do is add water. And because they boil most of the water they use with firewood, the new system spares the dwindling forests around these wretchedly poor hamlets.

"The price of the corn only goes up five percent .... while the quality goes up 100 percent," Chavez said. "This provides at least some nutritional level, because the poor people in this country don't even have money to buy beans."
